newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb leader fires back at her foes.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb leader fires back at her foes.

text.p: The president of Bosnia's Serb republic has decided to fight back against her political oppponents after moves by other Serb leaders to undermine her authority, diplomats said on Thursday.
Feisty comments delivered in a television interview showed Biljana Plavsic had no intention of bowing to her rivals based in the government seat of Pale, outside Sarajevo, they said.
"She wouldn't be going for it if she didn't think she had a chance of winning," said a Western diplomat, who asked not to be named.
"She may not be coming from a strong position but she is not going quietly."
Bosnian Serb officials in Pale have shut Plavsic out of decision-making after she blew the whistle on war profiteering by companies with links to the rest of the leadership.

In an interview with Banja Luka television, Plavsic accused Pale television, which is controlled by her rival Momcilo Krajisnik, of trying to bar her from appearing on the air while broadcasting calls for her resignation.
"My statements were refused by the television twice after some important events...," she said on Tuesday.
"I think incorrect things happened. Do not be surprised at my suspicions regarding the television...I have an idea who is behind this," she said.
"Believe me this amounts to the destruction of the country," she added.

Plavsic also slammed her associates for settling for what she called a flawed agreement on mutual cooperation with their patrons in neighbouring Yugoslavia. She said her vice-president had signed the pact without her approval.
Such a clear public attack on political leaders is virtually unheard of in Bosnian Serb territory, where authorities routinely stifle opposition.
At one point, a startled television presenter expressed surprise at Plavsic's sharp words, to which she replied, "Just make sure we don't run out of electricity."
The conflict reflected a long-time rift between the northwestern city of Banja Luka, where Plavsic is based, and the Pale leadership.
Many Serbs in Banja Luka view the Pale leaders as unaccountable and corrupt, unmoved by the plight of their impoverished population.
"There are a lot of angry people there who are probably encouraging Plavsic," said the diplomat.
But Serb political analysts say Plavsic, who played a secondary role during the war, has little leverage against Krajisnik and other well-connected Serb leaders in Pale.
Plavsic called on the police to investigate companies that smuggled fuel, cigarettes, coffee and alcohol during the war but her request was ignored.
Diplomats said Pale leaders had nominated Plavsic for president merely as a figurehead but it was unclear if they would tolerate her criticising them publicly.
Her allegations of war profiteering have cast the Pale leadership, which remains loyal to indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, in an embarrassing light.

Karadzic, accused of crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia, stepped down as president last year but diplomats say he still exerts influence from his office in Pale.
